resources.string: Clickify needs two permissions before it can do anything. It reads nothing from your screen, keeps every scenario on this device, and has no permission to use the internet.

Sending a touch to another app is the only thing Android lets an accessibility service do, and it is the only way this app can work. Android will warn you that the service "can observe your actions" — that warning covers every service of this kind. Clickify replays the taps you set up and looks at nothing.

Android blocks accessibility for apps installed from a file rather than from a store. Now that the toggle has refused once, the way through exists: Settings → Apps → Clickify → the ⋮ menu → Allow restricted settings. Then come back and turn the service on.
The markers, the floating control and the Stop button are drawn on top of whatever app you are automating. Without this there is nowhere to put them, and nowhere to put Stop.
A run puts a notification in the shade carrying Stop and Free the touch. Clickify will still run without it — it will just be quieter about the fact that it is running.

Advanced Protection refuses accessibility permission to every app that is not an assistive tool, and Clickify is an automation tool rather than an assistive one. There is no per-app exception and nothing here to retry. Turning Advanced Protection off is the only way, and that is your decision to make.
